items.stem: A micrometer screw gauge reads 0.03 mm with the jaws closed. A wire then gives a reading of 0.52 mm. What is the diameter of the wire?
items.markingKey: Subtract the zero error: 0.52 − 0.03.

items.stem: Explain why the number of significant figures in a calculated quantity should match those of the raw data.
items.answer: The precision of a result cannot be greater than the precision of the measurements used; quote it to the same (or one more) significant figures as the least precise data.
items.markingKey: precision limited by data [1]; same s.f. as least precise data [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why all the raw readings in a column should be recorded to the same number of decimal places.
items.answer: They are taken with the same instrument and so have the same precision; consistent decimal places show the resolution of that instrument.
items.markingKey: same instrument, same precision [1]; d.p. shows resolution [1] [2]

items.stem: A student times 20 oscillations of a mass on a spring three times: 48.2 s, 48.7 s, 47.8 s. Calculate the period of one oscillation.
items.markingKey: mean = 48.23 s; T = mean/20 = 2.41 s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A student times 10 oscillations of a mass on a spring three times: 12.4 s, 12.6 s, 12.0 s. Calculate the period and its absolute and percentage uncertainty, taking the uncertainty in the mean time as half the range.
items.markingKey: mean = 12.33 s [1]; half range = 0.30 s [1]; T = 1.23 s, ΔT = 0.03 s [1]; percentage 2.4% (same for T and total time) [1] [4]

items.stem: In a Paper 3 practical in Toronto, a candidate investigates how the period T of a mass on a spring depends on the mass m. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant. (b) State how many sets of readings should be taken and over what range.
items.answer: (a) same spring; same amplitude/displacement (b) At least six values spread over the widest possible range.
items.markingKey: (a) first control variable [1]; second control variable [1] [2] (b) six or more [1]; wide range [1] [2]

items.stem: Readings of a length are 54.2 cm, 54.6 cm and 54.4 cm. Which is the best way to record the result?
items.markingKey: Mean 54.4 cm; uncertainty = half the range = 0.2 cm.

items.stem: Describe how to measure the diameter of a wire accurately.
items.answer: Check the micrometer for zero error; close the jaws on the wire using the ratchet; take readings at several points along the wire and in different orientations; average and correct for zero error.
items.markingKey: zero error checked [1]; ratchet [1]; several positions and orientations, averaged [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a light gate and an electronic timer are often better than a stopwatch.
items.answer: They remove human reaction time, which is a large and variable source of error in short time intervals.
items.markingKey: removes reaction time [1]; significant for short times [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a light gate and an electronic timer are often better than a stopwatch. (b) Explain why the number of significant figures in a calculated quantity should match those of the raw data.
items.answer: (a) They remove human reaction time, which is a large and variable source of error in short time intervals. (b) The precision of a result cannot be greater than the precision of the measurements used; quote it to the same (or one more) significant figures as the least precise data.
items.markingKey: (a) removes reaction time [1]; significant for short times [1] [2] (b) precision limited by data [1]; same s.f. as least precise data [1] [2]

items.stem: In a Paper 3 practical in Lima, a candidate investigates how the period T of a mass on a spring depends on the mass m. (a) State the independent and dependent variables. (b) State two variables that should be kept constant.
items.answer: (a) m (independent); T (dependent) (b) same spring; same amplitude/displacement
items.markingKey: (a) m (independent); T (dependent) [1] (b) first control variable [1]; second control variable [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia investigates how the time for a ball to roll down a ramp depends on the height of the ramp. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant. (b) Draw the headings for a suitable results table.
items.answer: (a) same ball; same ramp length/surface (b) h / m | t₁ / s | t₂ / s | mean t / s
items.markingKey: (a) first control variable [1]; second control variable [1] [2] (b) quantity/unit headings [1]; repeats and derived columns [1] [2]

items.stem: A graph of T² against l for a simple pendulum is a straight line through the origin. What is the gradient?
items.answer: 4π²/g
items.markingKey: T² = (4π²/g) l.

items.stem: Explain why plotting a straight-line graph is useful in analysing an experiment.
items.answer: A straight line is easy to recognise and fit; the gradient and intercept give the constants in the relationship, and scatter or curvature shows errors or a wrong model.
items.markingKey: easy to judge linearity [1]; gradient/intercept give constants [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a scale such as 3 cm to represent 1 unit is not suitable on a graph.
items.answer: Awkward scales (multiples of 3, 7, etc.) make plotting and reading values difficult and lead to errors; scales of 1, 2 or 5 per division are used.
items.markingKey: awkward scale causes reading errors [1]; use 1, 2, 5 [1] [2]

items.stem: A student wants to test the relationship I = I₀ cos² θ using a straight-line graph. Which graph should be plotted?
items.answer: I against cos² θ
items.markingKey: Plot I (y-axis) against cos² θ (x-axis): gradient I₀, y-intercept zero.

items.stem: A student tests the relationship I = I₀ cos² θ. State the quantities to plot on each axis to give a straight line, and give expressions for the gradient and the y-intercept.
items.answer: y-axis I, x-axis cos² θ; gradient = I₀; intercept = zero
items.markingKey: axes [1]; gradient = I₀ [1]; intercept = zero [1] [3]

items.stem: A student investigates how the period T of a simple pendulum depends on its length l. (a) State how the gradient is used to find g. (b) Describe how to draw the line of best fit and find its gradient. (c) Suggest two further lengths that would improve the data set.
items.answer: (a) g = 4π²/gradient (b) Straight line with points balanced either side; use a triangle covering more than half the line. (c) e.g. 0.20 m and 1.10 m (extend range; at least six values)
items.markingKey: (a) g = 4π²/gradient [1] (b) balanced line [1]; large triangle [1] [2] (c) e.g. 0.20 m and 1.10 m (extend range; at least six values) [1]

items.stem: To test whether y = ax^n, which graph should be plotted?
items.answer: lg y against lg x
items.markingKey: lg y = n lg x + lg a: gradient n, intercept lg a.

items.stem: Describe how to find the uncertainty in the gradient of a straight-line graph.
items.answer: Plot error bars; draw the best-fit line and the worst acceptable straight line through the error bars; uncertainty = |best gradient − worst gradient|.
items.markingKey: error bars [1]; worst acceptable line [1]; difference of gradients [1] [3]

items.stem: In a Paper 3 results table, the time column shows only a single reading of each time, with no repeats. Identify what is wrong and state how it should be corrected.
items.answer: Repeat readings should be taken (at least twice) and the mean recorded, to reduce random error and identify anomalies.
items.markingKey: error identified [1]; correct practice stated [1] [2]

items.stem: In a Paper 3 results table, the student uses only four values of the independent variable over a narrow range. Identify what is wrong and state how it should be corrected.
items.answer: At least six values should be taken spread over as wide a range as possible.
items.markingKey: error identified [1]; correct practice stated [1] [2]

items.stem: A spring is loaded with masses m and the extension x recorded: m = 0.050 kg, x = 1.2 cm; m = 0.100 kg, x = 2.5 cm; m = 0.150 kg, x = 3.7 cm; m = 0.200 kg, x = 4.9 cm; m = 0.250 kg, x = 6.1 cm. (a) Determine the gradient of a graph of x (in m) against m. (b) Determine the spring constant.
items.answer: (a) 0.245 m kg⁻¹ (b) k = g/gradient = 40 N m⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) gradient = 0.245 m kg⁻¹ [1] (b) x = (g/k)m so k = g/gradient [1]; = 40 N m⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: Results for a simple pendulum: l = 0.200 m, T² = 0.798 s²; l = 0.400 m, T² = 1.595 s²; l = 0.600 m, T² = 2.393 s²; l = 0.800 m, T² = 3.190 s²; l = 1.000 m, T² = 3.988 s². A graph of T² against l is plotted. (a) Determine the gradient. (b) Use the gradient to determine g.
items.answer: (a) 3.99 s² m⁻¹ (b) g = 4π²/gradient = 9.9 m s⁻²

items.stem: A candidate in Hanoi measures the period T of a pendulum for lengths l of 0.30 m, 0.50 m, 0.70 m and 0.90 m. (a) Explain why T² is plotted against l rather than T against l. (b) Describe how to draw the line of best fit and find its gradient.

items.stem: A student tests whether T ∝ √m by calculating k = T/√m for two trials and gets 1.25 and 1.31. The percentage uncertainty in k is 3%. What should the student conclude?
options: The relationship is not supported because the values differ by more than 3%
No conclusion can be drawn about k
The relationship is supported because the values are close
items.answer: The relationship is not supported because the values differ by more than 3%

items.stem: Explain why a student should state a criterion before judging whether two k values agree.
items.answer: Without a criterion based on the experimental uncertainty, the judgement of "close enough" is arbitrary; the values should be compared with the percentage uncertainty in the data.
items.markingKey: criterion needed for a valid conclusion [1]; based on percentage uncertainty [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why two readings are insufficient to draw a valid conclusion about a relationship.
items.answer: With only two points any relationship can appear to hold or fail by chance; more readings over a wide range are needed to establish a trend and reduce random error.
items.markingKey: too few to establish trend [1]; random error/chance [1] [2]

items.stem: A student suggests that F is related to x by F = kx, where k is a constant. Two sets of readings are: x = 0.30 m, F = 0.75 N; and x = 0.80 m, F = 2.04 N. Calculate the value of k from the first set of readings.
items.markingKey: k = F/x = 0.75/0.30 = 2.5. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A student suggests that h is related to t by h = kt², where k is a constant. Two sets of readings are: t = 0.25 s, h = 0.40 m; and t = 0.75 s, h = 3.67 m. (a) Calculate two values of k. (b) Justify the number of significant figures you have given. (c) The student estimates the percentage uncertainty in the results as 10%. Explain whether the results support the suggested relationship.
items.answer: (a) 6.4 and 6.53 (b) 3 s.f., matching the raw data (c) percentage difference 2.0% is less than 10%, so the relationship is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) both k values [1] (b) s.f. same as raw data [1] (c) percentage difference = 2.0% [1]; valid comparison with 10% and conclusion [1] [4]

items.stem: A student times a falling object over a short distance with a hand-held stopwatch. Which is the most significant source of uncertainty?
options: Human reaction time in starting and stopping the stopwatch
items.answer: Human reaction time in starting and stopping the stopwatch
items.markingKey: Reaction time is large compared with a short interval.

items.stem: Which improvement reduces the random error in measuring the period of a pendulum?
options: Timing many oscillations and repeating the measurement
Using a stopwatch with more digits
items.answer: Timing many oscillations and repeating the measurement
items.markingKey: Larger total time and averaging reduce random error.

items.stem: Explain why "use a computer" is not an acceptable improvement in Paper 3, and give an example of how it could be made acceptable.
items.answer: It does not say what is measured or how; an acceptable version names the equipment and its purpose, e.g. "use a motion sensor connected to a data logger to measure the speed of the trolley".
items.markingKey: vague/does not state what or how [1]; specific example with purpose [1] [2]

items.stem: In one investigation, a student is (i) measuring the rebound height of a bouncing ball by eye against a metre rule and (ii) measuring the diameter of a wire once with a micrometer. For each, describe one limitation and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: (i) it is difficult to judge the maximum height (parallax and the ball moves quickly); improve: film the bounce against a scale and use frame-by-frame playback. (ii) the wire may not be uniform, so one reading may not be representative; improve: measure at several points along the wire and in different orientations, then average.
items.markingKey: (i) limitation [1]; improvement [1] (ii) limitation [1]; improvement [1] [4]

items.stem: In a Paper 3 investigation in Auckland, a student drops a paper cone from different heights and times its fall with a stopwatch to see whether it reaches terminal velocity. (a) Identify a limitation in releasing the cone and suggest an improvement. (b) Explain why vague suggestions such as "repeat more carefully" do not gain credit.
items.answer: (a) The cone may not be released from rest or may tilt; release it from a clamp/electromagnet or hold by a thread and burn it. (b) They do not identify a specific cause or a practical change to the method.
items.markingKey: (a) limitation [1]; improvement [1] [2] (b) They do not identify a specific cause or a practical change to the method [1]

items.stem: In Paper 3, which is NOT an acceptable improvement?
options: Take more readings and plot a graph
Use light gates connected to a timer
Use a fiducial marker at the centre of the swing
items.answer: "Be more careful"
items.markingKey: Improvements must be specific and practical.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a limitation and a source of uncertainty that is not significant.
items.answer: A limitation is a significant source of error in the specific experiment that affects the result; trivial issues (e.g. "human error") are not credited.
items.markingKey: limitation is significant/specific to experiment [1]; vague or trivial points not credited [1] [2]

items.stem: In one investigation, a student is (i) measuring the temperature of a liquid with a thermometer while it is heated and (ii) measuring the period of a pendulum by timing one oscillation. For each, describe one limitation and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: (i) the liquid may not be at a uniform temperature; improve: stir the liquid before each reading. (ii) one oscillation is too short to time accurately (reaction time); improve: time 20 oscillations and divide by 20, using a fiducial marker.
items.markingKey: (i) limitation [1]; improvement [1] (ii) limitation [1]; improvement [1] [4]

items.stem: In one investigation, a student is (i) measuring the diameter of a wire once with a micrometer and (ii) measuring the rebound height of a bouncing ball by eye against a metre rule. For each, describe one limitation and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: (i) the wire may not be uniform, so one reading may not be representative; improve: measure at several points along the wire and in different orientations, then average. (ii) it is difficult to judge the maximum height (parallax and the ball moves quickly); improve: film the bounce against a scale and use frame-by-frame playback.
items.markingKey: (i) limitation [1]; improvement [1] (ii) limitation [1]; improvement [1] [4]

items.stem: In one investigation, a student is (i) timing the fall of a paper cone dropped from a height of 1.5 m with a stopwatch and (ii) measuring the distance a ball rolls along a carpet. For each, describe one limitation and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: (i) the time is short, so reaction time causes a large percentage uncertainty; improve: use a longer drop height or a video camera with a timer / light gates. (ii) the ball may veer to one side and the carpet surface is uneven; improve: use a guide rail / a smoother uniform surface.
items.markingKey: (i) limitation [1]; improvement [1] (ii) limitation [1]; improvement [1] [4]

items.stem: What is the resolution of a typical metre rule?
items.answer: 1 mm
items.markingKey: Smallest scale division.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe how to measure the diameter of a wire accurately. (b) Explain why a light gate and an electronic timer are often better than a stopwatch.
items.answer: (a) Check the micrometer for zero error; close the jaws on the wire using the ratchet; take readings at several points along the wire and in different orientations; average and correct for zero error. (b) They remove human reaction time, which is a large and variable source of error in short time intervals.

items.stem: When drawing a line of best fit through plotted points, which is correct?
options: The points should be balanced on either side of the line
The line should join each point to the next
The line must pass through the first and last points
The line must pass through the origin
items.answer: The points should be balanced on either side of the line
items.markingKey: A line of best fit balances the scatter.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a scale such as 3 cm to represent 1 unit is not suitable on a graph. (b) Describe how to find the uncertainty in the gradient of a straight-line graph.
items.answer: (a) Awkward scales (multiples of 3, 7, etc.) make plotting and reading values difficult and lead to errors; scales of 1, 2 or 5 per division are used. (b) Plot error bars; draw the best-fit line and the worst acceptable straight line through the error bars; uncertainty = |best gradient − worst gradient|.
items.markingKey: (a) awkward scale causes reading errors [1]; use 1, 2, 5 [1] [2] (b) error bars [1]; worst acceptable line [1]; difference of gradients [1] [3]

items.stem: A student wants to test the relationship T = 2π√(l/g) using a straight-line graph. Which graph should be plotted?
items.answer: T² against l
items.markingKey: Plot T² (y-axis) against l (x-axis): gradient 4π²/g, y-intercept zero.

items.stem: A student tests the relationship y = ax^n. State the quantities to plot on each axis to give a straight line, and give expressions for the gradient and the y-intercept.
items.answer: y-axis lg y, x-axis lg x; gradient = n; intercept = lg a

items.stem: A candidate in Karachi measures the period T of a pendulum for lengths l of 0.30 m, 0.50 m, 0.70 m and 0.90 m. (a) For l = 0.90 m, T = 1.91 s. (d) Suggest two further lengths that would improve the data set.
items.answer: (a) 3.65 s² (b) g = 4π²/gradient (c) Straight line with points balanced either side; use a triangle covering more than half the line. (d) e.g. 0.20 m and 1.10 m (extend range; at least six values)

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Two values of a constant k are 4.82 and 4.96. What is the percentage difference between them? (b) A length is measured as 25.0 cm with an uncertainty of ±0.5 cm. Its percentage uncertainty is …

Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a student should state a criterion before judging whether two k values agree. (b) Explain why two readings are insufficient to draw a valid conclusion about a relationship.
items.answer: (a) Without a criterion based on the experimental uncertainty, the judgement of "close enough" is arbitrary; the values should be compared with the percentage uncertainty in the data. (b) With only two points any relationship can appear to hold or fail by chance; more readings over a wide range are needed to establish a trend and reduce random error.
items.markingKey: (a) criterion needed for a valid conclusion [1]; based on percentage uncertainty [1] [2] (b) too few to establish trend [1]; random error/chance [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how error bars help to judge whether a straight line through the origin is consistent with data. (b) Explain why a student should state a criterion before judging whether two k values agree.
items.answer: (a) If a straight line through the origin can be drawn passing through all (or most) of the error bars, the data are consistent with proportionality within the uncertainties. (b) Without a criterion based on the experimental uncertainty, the judgement of "close enough" is arbitrary; the values should be compared with the percentage uncertainty in the data.
items.markingKey: (a) line through error bars [1]; consistent within uncertainty [1] [2] (b) criterion needed for a valid conclusion [1]; based on percentage uncertainty [1] [2]

items.stem: From a graph with error bars, the line of best fit has gradient 1.56 and y-intercept 1.5. The worst acceptable line has gradient 1.68 and y-intercept 1.95 (same units). State the gradient and intercept with their absolute uncertainties, and calculate the percentage uncertainty in the gradient.
items.answer: gradient = 1.56 ± 0.1; intercept = 1.5 ± 0.5; 8.0%
items.markingKey: Δgradient = |1.56 − 1.68| = 0.1 [1]; Δintercept = 0.5 [1]; percentage = 8.0% [1] [3]

items.stem: A student suggests that h is related to t by h = kt², where k is a constant. Two sets of readings are: t = 0.20 s, h = 0.196 m; and t = 0.60 s, h = 1.80 m. Work out the value of k from the first set of readings.
items.markingKey: k = h/t² = 0.196/0.20 (with root or square as needed) = 4.9. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A candidate in Hanoi investigates a mass on a spring. With m = 0.100 kg the period is 0.82 s; with m = 0.300 kg it is 1.48 s. It is suggested that T = k√m. (a) Calculate two values of k. (b) Identify two limitations of the procedure.
items.answer: (a) 2.59 and 2.70 s kg⁻¹ᐟ² (b) only two values of m; difficult to judge start/end of oscillation; spring oscillates sideways

items.stem: For a mass-spring system, T = 1.10 s when m = 0.100 kg and T = 1.85 s when m = 0.300 kg. The relationship T = k√m is to be tested. (a) Calculate two values of k. (b) The period was found by timing 10 oscillations with an uncertainty of 0.2 s. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the first period. items.answer: (a) 3.48 and 3.37 s kg⁻¹ᐟ² (b) 1.8% (c) percentage difference in k = 3.0%, greater than 1.8%, so the relationship is not supported.

items.stem: Explain why improving the precision of an instrument does not always improve the result.
items.answer: If the dominant uncertainty is elsewhere (e.g. reaction time or difficulty judging the moment), a more precise instrument does not reduce the overall uncertainty.
items.markingKey: dominant uncertainty elsewhere [1]; precision of instrument not limiting [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Mumbai is measuring the rebound height of a bouncing ball by eye against a metre rule. Identify a significant limitation of this method and suggest a specific improvement.
items.answer: Limitation: it is difficult to judge the maximum height (parallax and the ball moves quickly). Improvement: film the bounce against a scale and use frame-by-frame playback.
items.markingKey: limitation specific to the experiment [1]; matching, practical improvement [1] [2]

items.stem: In one investigation, a student is (i) timing the fall of a paper cone dropped from a height of 1.5 m with a stopwatch and (ii) measuring the diameter of a wire once with a micrometer. For each, describe one limitation and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: (i) the time is short, so reaction time causes a large percentage uncertainty; improve: use a longer drop height or a video camera with a timer / light gates. (ii) the wire may not be uniform, so one reading may not be representative; improve: measure at several points along the wire and in different orientations, then average.
items.markingKey: (i) limitation [1]; improvement [1] (ii) limitation [1]; improvement [1] [4]
